34 A copper wire of length 2 m has a circular cross-section. There is a constant current in the wire
when it is connected to a mobile phone in order to charge the battery.
The wire has a fault. A 1 m length of the wire has half the diameter of the other 1 m length.
The power dissipated in the thicker length of wire is P.
What is the power dissipated in the thinner length of wire?
A
P
4
1
B
P
2
1
C
2P
D
4P

hints: Notice the wording constant current in the wire - the 1 m thicker section and 1 m thinner section are in series, so $I$ is the same for comparing $P = I^2R$.
Connect diameter to resistance with $R = \rho L / A$ and $A = \pi d^2/4$ for the circular cross-section, with the same $\rho$ and $L = 1 \text{ m}$ for both sections.
Combine the area change when $d$ is halved with $P = I^2R$ at constant $I$ to find the ratio of the thinner-section power to $P$.
walkthrough: The two 1 m lengths form one continuous wire, so the same constant current $I$ flows through the thicker and thinner sections.
For each section, resistance is $R = \rho L / A$, where $\rho$ is the resistivity of copper, $L = 1 \text{ m}$ is the same, and $A = \pi d^2/4$.
Halving the diameter gives $A_{thin} = \pi (d/2)^2/4 = (1/4)\pi d^2/4 = A_{thick}/4$, so the cross-sectional area is quartered.
Therefore $R_{thin} = \rho L / (A_{thick}/4) = 4R_{thick}$; the thinner 1 m length has four times the resistance.
With the same $I$, $P = I^2R$, so $P_{thin} = I^2(4R_{thick}) = 4P_{thick} = 4P$. This is option D.

A.explanation: This would imply resistance decreases to one quarter, but halving diameter decreases area and increases resistance.

B.explanation: This treats resistance as proportional to diameter, whereas resistance is inversely proportional to area which depends on $d^2$.

C.explanation: This doubles the power, using the diameter ratio directly instead of squaring it to find the area ratio.

D.explanation: With the same current, $P = I^2R$ and quarter area gives four times resistance, so power is $4P$.
